vjimc-2007-cat2-01.title: Inductive choice in a countable base
vjimc-2007-cat2-01.body:
Let $U_1,U_2,U_3,\dots$ be an enumeration of all open squares $(a,b)\times(c,d)$ with rational $0\le a<b\le1$, $0\le c<d\le1$; there are countably many, and every nonempty relatively open subset of $[0,1]^2$ contains one of them.

Choose points $P_k=(x_k,y_k)$ inductively. Having chosen $P_1,\dots,P_{k-1}$, write $U_k=(a,b)\times(c,d)$. The interval $(a,b)$ is infinite, so we can pick $x_k\in(a,b)$ different from $x_1,\dots,x_{k-1}$; similarly pick $y_k\in(c,d)$ different from $y_1,\dots,y_{k-1}$. Then $P_k\in U_k$.

Let $A=\{P_k:k\ge1\}$.
- $A$ is dense: every nonempty open subset of $[0,1]^2$ contains some $U_k$, hence the point $P_k$.
- All $x_k$ are distinct, so a vertical line $x=\text{const}$ contains at most one point of $A$; all $y_k$ are distinct, so the same holds for horizontal lines. ∎

vjimc-2007-cat2-01.title: Irrational rotations
vjimc-2007-cat2-01.body:
Let $\{t\}$ denote the fractional part and put
$$A=\{(\{n\sqrt2\},\{n\sqrt3\}) : n=1,2,3,\dots\}.$$
If $\{n\sqrt2\}=\{m\sqrt2\}$ then $(n-m)\sqrt2\in\mathbb Z$, so $n=m$; hence different points of $A$ have different first coordinates, and likewise different second coordinates. So every vertical or horizontal line meets $A$ at most once.

The numbers $1,\sqrt2,\sqrt3$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$ (if $a+b\sqrt2+c\sqrt3=0$ with rational $a,b,c$, squaring $a+b\sqrt2=-c\sqrt3$ gives $a^2+2b^2-3c^2+2ab\sqrt2=0$, so $ab=0$, and each remaining case forces a rational square root of $2$, $3$ or $\frac32$ unless all coefficients vanish). By Kronecker's theorem on simultaneous approximation, the sequence $(\{n\sqrt2\},\{n\sqrt3\})$ is then dense in $[0,1]^2$ (it is even equidistributed by Weyl's criterion).

(Independence of $1,\alpha,\beta$ over $\mathbb Q$ really is needed: for $\alpha=\sqrt2$, $\beta=\sqrt2+1$, all points lie on the diagonal $x=y$.) ∎

vjimc-2007-cat2-02.title: Eigenvalues of a skew-symmetric matrix
vjimc-2007-cat2-02.body:
Put $S=A-\frac12I$. Then $S^t=A^t-\frac12I=(I-A)-\frac12I=-S$, so $S$ is skew-symmetric and $A=\frac12I+S$.

**Eigenvalues of $S$ are purely imaginary.** If $Sv=\lambda v$ with $v\in\mathbb C^n\setminus\{0\}$, then $\bar v^tSv=\lambda\,\bar v^tv=\lambda\|v\|^2$. Taking the complex conjugate and transposing (a scalar), and using that $S$ is real, $\overline{\bar v^tSv}=v^tS\bar v=(v^tS\bar v)^t=\bar v^tS^tv=-\bar v^tSv$. Hence $\bar\lambda\|v\|^2=-\lambda\|v\|^2$, so $\bar\lambda=-\lambda$.

The characteristic polynomial of $S$ has real coefficients, so its non-real roots come in conjugate pairs $\pm ir_k$ ($r_k>0$, $k=1,\dots,s$) with equal multiplicities, and the only real root possible is $0$ (with multiplicity $n-2s$). The eigenvalues of $A=\frac12I+S$ are $\frac12+\lambda$ for the eigenvalues $\lambda$ of $S$ (with multiplicity), and the determinant is their product:
$$\det A=\left(\frac12\right)^{n-2s}\prod_{k=1}^s\left(\frac12+ir_k\right)\left(\frac12-ir_k\right)=\left(\frac12\right)^{n-2s}\prod_{k=1}^s\left(\frac14+r_k^2\right)>0. \qquad ∎$$

vjimc-2007-cat2-02.title: Continuity argument
vjimc-2007-cat2-02.body:
For $t\in[0,1]$ let $A_t=\frac12I+t\,S$ with $S=A-\frac12I$ (skew-symmetric, as $A+A^t=I$). For a real vector $x\ne0$,
$$x^tA_tx=\tfrac12\|x\|^2+t\,x^tSx=\tfrac12\|x\|^2>0,$$
because $x^tSx$ is a scalar equal to its transpose $x^tS^tx=-x^tSx$, hence $0$. Therefore $A_tx\ne0$ for all $x\neq 0$, i.e. $A_t$ is invertible and $\det A_t\ne0$ for every $t\in[0,1]$.

The function $t\mapsto\det A_t$ is a polynomial, hence continuous, it never vanishes on $[0,1]$, and $\det A_0=2^{-n}>0$. By the intermediate value theorem $\det A_1=\det A>0$. ∎

vjimc-2007-cat2-03.title: Cyclic difference function
vjimc-2007-cat2-03.body:
(Here $x$ is required to satisfy $x,x+h\in[0,1]$.)

**Measurability.** The set $K=\{(x,h)\in[0,1]^2: x+h\le1,\ f(x+h)=f(x)\}$ is closed (as $f$ is continuous) and bounded, hence compact. $A$ is its projection onto the $h$-axis, a continuous image of a compact set, so $A$ is compact, in particular Borel and Lebesgue measurable.

**Key claim: for every $h\in[0,1]$, $h\in A$ or $1-h\in A$.** Extend $f$ to a $1$-periodic function $F$ on $\mathbb R$; since $f(0)=f(1)$, $F$ is continuous. Let $g(x)=F(x+h)-F(x)$ for $x\in[0,1]$; it is continuous. Let $f$ attain its minimum on $[0,1]$ at $x_0$ and its maximum at $x_1$. Then $F$ has the same minimum and maximum on $\mathbb R$, so $g(x_0)\ge0\ge g(x_1)$, and by the intermediate value theorem $g(x_2)=0$ for some $x_2\in[0,1]$.
- If $x_2+h\le1$, then $f(x_2+h)=f(x_2)$, so $h\in A$.
- If $x_2+h>1$, then $y=x_2+h-1\in[0,1]$, $F(x_2+h)=f(y)$, and $y+(1-h)=x_2$; thus $f(y+(1-h))=f(y)$ and $1-h\in A$.

**Measure.** Let $B=\{h\in[0,1]:1-h\in A\}$, the reflection of $A$ about $\frac12$; it is measurable with $\lambda(B)=\lambda(A)$. By the claim, $A\cup B=[0,1]$, so
$$1\le\lambda(A)+\lambda(B)=2\lambda(A),$$
i.e. $\lambda(A)\ge\frac12$. ∎

vjimc-2007-cat2-04.title: Coupling via a cube
vjimc-2007-cat2-04.body:
Let $S=\{1,\dots,n\}$. For $t\in[0,1]$ and $A\subseteq S$ let
$$I_{t,A}=\prod_{j=1}^n I^{(j)}_{t,A}\subseteq[0,1]^n,\qquad I^{(j)}_{t,A}=\begin{cases}[0,t)&j\in A,\\ [t,1]&j\notin A.\end{cases}$$
Its volume is $t^{|A|}(1-t)^{n-|A|}$. For fixed $t$ the boxes $I_{t,A}$ ($A\subseteq S$) are pairwise disjoint: a point $x$ lies in $I_{t,A}$ exactly for $A=A_t(x):=\{j:x_j<t\}$. Hence
$$f(t)=\operatorname{vol}\Big(\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal F}I_{t,A}\Big)=\operatorname{vol}\{x\in[0,1]^n: A_t(x)\in\mathcal F\}.$$

Let $t_1<t_2$. For every $x$, $A_{t_1}(x)=\{j:x_j<t_1\}\subseteq\{j:x_j<t_2\}=A_{t_2}(x)$, so if $A_{t_1}(x)\in\mathcal F$ then $A_{t_2}(x)\in\mathcal F$ by the hypothesis on $\mathcal F$. Thus
$$\{x: A_{t_1}(x)\in\mathcal F\}\subseteq\{x:A_{t_2}(x)\in\mathcal F\},$$
and comparing volumes $f(t_1)\le f(t_2)$. (In probabilistic language: choose $x$ uniformly in $[0,1]^n$; then each $j$ belongs to $A_t(x)$ independently with probability $t$, $f(t)=P(A_t\in\mathcal F)$, and $A_t$ grows with $t$.) ∎

vjimc-2007-cat2-04.title: Differentiate and pair sets
vjimc-2007-cat2-04.body:
Write $w_A(t)=t^{|A|}(1-t)^{n-|A|}$. For each $A$,
$$w_A'(t)=|A|\,t^{|A|-1}(1-t)^{n-|A|}-(n-|A|)\,t^{|A|}(1-t)^{n-|A|-1}=\sum_{j\in A}u_A(t)-\sum_{j\notin A}u_{A\cup\{j\}}(t),$$
where $u_B(t)=t^{|B|-1}(1-t)^{n-|B|}$ for nonempty $B$ (note $u_{A\cup\{j\}}=t^{|A|}(1-t)^{n-|A|-1}$ for $j\notin A$). Summing over $A\in\mathcal F$,
$$f'(t)=\sum_{(A,j):\,A\in\mathcal F,\ j\in A}u_A(t)\;-\sum_{(A,j):\,A\in\mathcal F,\ j\notin A}u_{A\cup\{j\}}(t).$$
The map $(A,j)\mapsto(A\cup\{j\},j)$ sends the pairs of the second sum injectively to pairs $(B,j)$ with $j\in B$, and $B=A\cup\{j\}\in\mathcal F$ since $\mathcal F$ is closed upwards. So every negative term cancels against a distinct positive term, and
$$f'(t)=\sum_{\substack{B\in\mathcal F,\ j\in B\\ B\setminus\{j\}\notin\mathcal F}}t^{|B|-1}(1-t)^{n-|B|}\ \ge 0\qquad(0\le t\le 1).$$
Therefore $f$ is nondecreasing on $[0,1]$. ∎
